title: 1,800 People Help Move Castle in Japan
paragraphs: In August 2026, around 1,800 volunteers in northern Japan used ropes to pull part of a historic castle back toward its original location.

The building was the keep, or main tower, of Hirosaki Castle in Aomori Prefecture. The three-story tower was built in 1810 and weighs about 360 tonnes. Because it is an important cultural property, it could not be taken apart. Instead, it was moved using a traditional Japanese technique called "hikiya." In this method, a building is placed on rollers and pulled from one place to another without being dismantled.

This was not the first time the tower had been moved. In 2015, it was moved away from its original position so that a stone wall beneath it, which had been damaged by an earthquake, could be repaired. Volunteers also helped with that move. The repairs to the stone wall were finally completed in December 2024, so the tower could begin its journey back.

Over a weekend in August, the volunteers took turns pulling the tower with 30-meter-long ropes, working in groups of 80 people at a time. On the first day, they moved the tower about 1.13 meters, and on the second day, about 1.09 meters more. In total, they moved it just over two meters.

The work was not finished, however. About 4,100 people were expected to take part in pulling the tower during the rest of August, moving it about five meters in total. The remaining 73 meters would be covered using machines, and the tower was expected to reach its final position before the end of the year.

The event attracted attention from around the world, and videos of the volunteers pulling the tower were widely shared online. For many people, it showed how communities in Japan work together to protect their history.
